name: A Primer of Indian Logic
author: S. Kuppuswami Sastri
description: S. Kuppuswami Sastri’s A Primer of Indian Logic serves as a comprehensive educational bridge between classical Sanskrit scholarship and modern English-speaking students by providing a systematic introduction to the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophical system. The work is structured around the Tarkasamgraha of Annambhatta, offering the original text in Devanagari and transliteration alongside a detailed, comparative exposition of Indian epistemology and metaphysics. Sastri’s primary purpose is to elucidate the science of methodical reasoning, which encompasses both the inductive observation of the Vaiśeṣika school and the deductive syllogistic framework of the Nyāya school. By meticulously defining the seven categories (padārthas) and the sources of valid knowledge (pramāņas), the author demonstrates that Indian logic is not merely a formal grammar of thought, but a spiritual discipline aimed at achieving final emancipation (mukti). Ultimately, the text highlights the unique syncretism of Indian systems, where logic, psychology, and ontology are harmoniously integrated to facilitate a rigorous investigation of truth and reality.
short: Introductory exposition of Indian logical method, categories, inference, and debate using the Tarkasangraha tradition.

name: An Elementary Treatise on Mimamsa
author: Laugakshi Bhaskara
description: This document is a translated excerpt from the Artha-samgraha, a foundational Sanskrit manual authored by Laugakshi Bhaskara in the late 17th century to introduce students to the Mimamsa-sastra. The text focuses on the systematic interpretation of the Vedas, specifically the Karma-kanda or the section regarding sacrificial action, by defining Dharma as a duty validated by scripture to achieve a purposeful result. The author meticulously categorises the Veda into five parts—injunctions, mantras, names, prohibitions, and explanatory statements—while detailing the linguistic mechanics of Bhavana, or the "productive energy" that compels a person to perform religious acts. Central to this treatise are the six means of proof (such as direct statement and interdependence) used to determine the hierarchical relationship between primary sacrifices and their subsidiary parts. Ultimately, the work serves as a logical framework for constructing ritual manuals, aiming to prove that every syllable of the sacred texts possesses a visible, practical utility in the pursuit of spiritual and worldly rewards.
short: Accessible introduction to Mimamsa principles, Vedic injunctions, and hermeneutical reasoning.

Hosted by the Bodha organisation, the platform organises deep intellectual enquiries into classical Indian schools of thought through a structured mix of academic essays, research notes, and primary scriptures. The primary objective is to facilitate a comprehensive cultural immersion by connecting ancient logical traditions with modern scholarly research. Consequently, the source acts as both an educational archive and a contemporary research hub for those seeking to understand the fundamental nature of truth within the Darshana tradition.
short: Study of Navya-Nyaya truth theory and the epistemic conditions of valid cognition.

name: A Scheme for Knowledge Representation in Samskritam
author: P. Ramanujan
description: This paper explores the potential of utilizing traditional Samskritam shastraic literature as a sophisticated framework for knowledge representation in modern Artificial Intelligence. By examining the structural precision of ancient linguistic and logical systems—specifically Vyakarana (grammar), Nyaya (logic), and Mimamsa (interpretation)—the author proposes a technical scheme consisting of a comprehensive lexicon, an exhaustive knowledge base of sutras, and advanced analysis modules. The text emphasizes that the self-inference characteristics of Sanskrit and its rigorous ontological categorisation offer a unique, ready-made model for solving complex problems in Natural Language Processing and machine understanding. Ultimately, the work serves as a visionary bridge between classical Indian sciences and the contemporary requirements of Expert Systems and computational linguistics.

description: In this academic article, Dilip Loundo explores the soteriological dimensions of the Sanskrit grammatical form known as ātmanepada, moving beyond mere linguistics to investigate its deeper philosophical and ontological implications. Drawing primarily on the Vākyapadīya by Bhartṛhari, the author argues that this specific verbal diathesis is not merely a technical rule but a transformative tool that suggests a purportful unity between the agent of an action and its results. By examining the concept of samvidhāna, or the act of making provisions, Loundo demonstrates how the usage of ātmanepada helps a practitioner transition from a fragmented worldly perspective to a realisation of the non-dual Brahman. Ultimately, the text positions traditional Indian grammar as a spiritual discipline capable of unveiling the foundational oneness that exists beneath the multiplicity of linguistic forms and human experiences.

The text is systematically divided into lessons that address the alphabet and phonetics (Svara and Vyañjana), the nuances of sentence structure and inflection, and the complex principles of euphonic combination known as Sandhi. By integrating grammatical theory with flashcards and exercises, the guide equips students with the essential tools to navigate Monier-Williams’ etymological dictionary and the Dhātu-Pātha. Ultimately, the course serves as a bridge to the study of sacred scriptures, encouraging learners to look past literal translations to find the profound spiritual meaning embedded within the etymology of the original Sanskrit roots.

It serves as an extensive manual for religious ritual and temple architecture, detailing the precise methods for consecrating idols, constructing sacred edifices, and performing purification rites. Beyond theology, the text encompasses a vast array of secular and practical subjects, including military strategy, the medicinal properties of plants, the governance of a kingdom, and the complex laws of inheritance and judicial disputes. Ultimately, the work functions as a spiritual and worldly guide, aiming to provide the reader with the tools for both earthly prosperity and final emancipation from the cycle of existence.

name: Aitareya Upanishad
description: This 1923 publication represents the fifth volume in a series dedicated to providing an English translation of the Aitareya and Taittiriya Upanishads, accompanied by the influential commentary of Sri Sankara. Published in Madras by V. C. Seshacharri and dedicated to the prominent theosophist Dr Annie Besant, the work aims to bridge the gap between ancient Sanskrit philosophy and modern English-speaking audiences through a rigorous yet accessible rendering. The text emphasizes that emancipation is achieved through knowledge alone, specifically the realization of the A'tman or the Supreme Self, rather than through ritualistic actions or worldly deeds. Within these pages, the unity of Brahman is explored as the ultimate reality that transcends the distinctions of the material world, offering a path to fearlessness and immortality by removing the illusions of ignorance. Ultimately, the volume serves as both a scholarly resource and a spiritual guide, preserving the profound insights of Eastern religious philosophy for a global readership.

Central to its philosophy is the idea that a ruler’s success depends on restraint of the senses and the diligent oversight of a vast espionage network to maintain internal and external security. name: Advanced Textbook of Hindu Religion and Ethics
description: This 1903 textbook from the Central Hindu College in Benares presents a comprehensive overview of Sanatana Dharma, framing it as an ancient yet flexible system of religion, science, and ethics. The text meticulously outlines the hierarchy of sacred literature, beginning with the Vedas (Shruti) and extending through the laws of the Smritis, the philosophical Six Darshanas, and the instructive narratives of the Puranas and Itihasas. Central to its teachings are the metaphysical concepts of Karma and the reincarnation of the Jivatma, which move toward the ultimate goal of achieving unity with the Supreme Self through knowledge and devotion. By explaining the Varnashrama system of social classes and life stages, the source seeks to provide a rational, orderly guide for Aryan living and moral conduct. Ultimately, the work serves as a spiritual and ethical roadmap designed to foster pure reason, compassion, and self-realisation in the modern student.
short: More advanced textbook on Hindu ethics, doctrine, discipline, and moral reasoning.
